meaning: Amusement Device Inspection Procedures Scheme. The UK scheme for checking that rides used by the public are safe. Our rig counts as a ride.
Declaration of Operational Compliance. The certificate an ADIPS inspector gives once the rig passes. No paying riders without it.
The Health and Safety Executive's guidance on fairground and amusement rides. ADIPS follows it.
Insurance that pays out if a member of the public is hurt or their property is damaged because of us.
Portable Appliance Testing. A safety test for plug-in electrical kit, recorded with a sticker on each item.
Value Added Tax. Depending on how SmartMotion is set up, public prices may need to include 20% VAT.
UK data protection law. It covers how we collect, store and use customers' personal details.
The law on reporting certain workplace accidents and injuries to the Health and Safety Executive.
Automated External Defibrillator. The portable machine used if someone's heart stops.
Six degrees of freedom. The rig can move in all six directions: tilt forward and back, tilt side to side, turn, and slide forward, sideways and up and down.
Permission from a software company to use their game for paid rides. Normal shop-bought copies don't allow it.
Free motion program (non-commercial use only) that reads the game and tells the rig how to move. Our own SmartMotion Motion replaces it for SmartMotion Flight.
The UK Intellectual Property Office. It's where you check and register trademarks such as a business name.
A limited company. A separate legal business, so the owners' personal money is protected if things go wrong.
An international customs document that lets equipment travel abroad temporarily without paying import tax.
The point where money coming in covers all the costs. About £3,900 a month for SmartMotion.
How much of the available ride time is actually booked, shown as a percentage.
The standard 3D printing file. Open it in your slicer (Anycubic Slicer, Cura, PrusaSlicer) to print it. It can't easily be edited.
An editable CAD file. Open it in Fusion 360, Onshape, FreeCAD or SolidWorks to change the design properly.
The program that turns a 3D model into layer-by-layer instructions for the printer (Anycubic Slicer Next for the Kobra 3).
The pattern printed inside a part to save plastic. 15 to 30% is normal; more makes it heavier and stronger.
A wavy infill pattern that is equally strong in every direction and prints quickly.
The easiest printing plastic. Stiff and neat, but softens at around 55°C.
A tougher, slightly flexible plastic. Good for clips, brackets and anything that gets knocked.
A small brass threaded sleeve pressed into a printed hole with a soldering iron, so screws can go in and out many times.
Part of a print that sticks out over thin air. Up to about 45° prints fine; flatter needs supports.
The first layer squashing outwards slightly, making the bottom edge a little bigger than designed.
The small gap left between parts that must fit together, so they don't jam.
Virtual reality. You wear a headset (like the Meta Quest 3) and the game surrounds you, so you look around by turning your head.
The browser feature that lets a web page run in VR. SmartMotion Flight uses it to work on the Quest without installing anything.
Live numbers from the game (tilt, speed, forces) sent out so the motion rig can move to match what the pilot would feel.
The free game engine the Windows version of SmartMotion Flight is built with. It draws the graphics using your PC's graphics card.
A fast way for programs to send live numbers to each other on a PC or network. The game uses it to feed the motion rig.
The standard that lets games talk to VR headsets like the Meta Quest 3, here through the Meta Quest Link app.
Claude working directly in the SmartMotion repository: it can read and change the files, run checks and publish updates. Start a session on the Smartmotion-Repo repository and ask in plain English.
The website that stores the SmartMotion repository (all the files, the plan and the game). The game download is kept there too, so you need to be signed in.
Meta's app that connects the Quest 3 headset to the laptop (by cable or Wi-Fi, called Air Link), so the laptop runs the game and the headset shows it.
Our own program that moves the simulator with SmartMotion Flight. It replaces FlyPT Mover: it reads the game, works out the seat movement and sends it to the Motion4Sim controller.
Turning what the aircraft does into small seat movements the rig can actually make, so the rider feels the right pushes without the rig running out of travel.
After a quick movement the seat drifts slowly back to the middle, too gently to notice, so it has room for the next one.
Leaning the seat slowly so gravity pushes the rider the way a lasting force would, for example back into the seat on take-off.
A Motion4Sim controller setting: our program says where the seat should be (tilt and movement), and the controller works out how long each actuator must be.
The company that makes the rig's motion controller (the box that drives the actuator motors), and its set-up program, the Motion4Sim Dashboard.
How Windows names a USB connection to a device such as the motion controller, e.g. COM3.
In VR the headset moves with the seat. The game cancels that movement out, so the cockpit stays still around you while the rig moves.
SmartMotion Motion working on screen only: the 3D picture moves, but nothing is sent to the rig.
